Neonates of Tropidurus itambere emerge from parchment-shelled eggs at a remarkably modest size, with the snout-vent length at birth measuring approximately 2.85 cm [Lb = approximately 2.85 cm]. This small body size at hatching, typical of many tropidurid lizards, places the young at a competitive disadvantage in the rocky outcrop habitats they inhabit, where predation pressure from birds and snakes is intense. The initial growth trajectory is rapid, as young-of-year individuals must invest heavily in somatic development to reach the minimum size threshold required for reproductive activity. Field surveys conducted in the Cerrado region of southeastern Brazil indicate that the onset of sexual maturation in females is triggered once they attain a snout-vent length of roughly 5.5 cm [Lp = roughly 5.5 cm], whereas males begin their pubertal development at a slightly larger body size, with records showing puberty initiating at approximately 5.6 cm [Lp = approximately 5.6 cm]. This subtle sexual dimorphism in maturation size likely reflects divergent selective pressures on males and females, with males needing to achieve a competitive body size for territorial defense before they can successfully court mates. The period from birth to the attainment of these pubertal thresholds is strongly influenced by local thermal conditions, as metabolic processes driving growth are temperature-dependent in this ectothermic species. Consequently, individuals born early in the rainy season benefit from extended periods of optimal basking temperatures, allowing them to reach puberty sooner than those emerging later in the year, a pattern that has been documented in other saxicolous lizards inhabiting seasonal tropical environments. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that these size thresholds are relatively conservative within the genus Tropidurus.

At a constant ambient temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the time required for juvenile female Tropidurus itambere to reach sexual maturity from the point of hatching has been documented at 170 days [tp = 170 days]. This relatively protracted developmental period, spanning nearly six months, reflects the slow pace of life history typical of small-bodied insectivorous lizards inhabiting resource-limited environments. For juvenile males raised under identical thermal and dietary conditions, the corresponding duration from birth to the onset of puberty is notably shorter, recorded at 132 days [tp = 132 days] at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This sex-specific divergence in developmental timing, with males maturing approximately 38 days earlier than females, is a recurring pattern across many squamate lineages and is often interpreted as a consequence of differential selective regimes operating on the two sexes. Males may benefit from early maturation by securing territories and establishing dominance hierarchies before the peak breeding season arrives, while females may delay maturity to allocate more resources to achieving a larger body size that enhances clutch volume and offspring survival. The experiments were conducted in environmental chambers with a 12-hour photoperiod, and lizards were fed ad libitum on domestic crickets dusted with calcium and vitamin supplements. Growth curves were fitted to weekly measurements of snout-vent length and body mass to precisely identify the inflection point corresponding to gonadal activation, which was subsequently confirmed through dissection of a subset of individuals at regular intervals throughout the study period. These data provide a robust baseline for understanding how temperature mediates the timing of key life history transitions in this species.

Adult body size in Tropidurus itambere exhibits moderate sexual dimorphism, with females reaching a smaller ultimate snout-vent length than males. Long-term mark-recapture studies conducted over a five-year period have documented that females attain a maximum asymptotic snout-vent length of approximately 7.95 cm [Li = approximately 7.95 cm], a value that is consistent across multiple populations within the species' range and shows little interannual variation. In contrast, males continue somatic growth for a longer period following sexual maturation and ultimately achieve a larger adult body size, with the most elderly and dominant individuals recorded at a snout-vent length of 9.35 cm [Li = 9.35 cm]. This size differential is thought to arise from a combination of sexual selection favoring larger males in agonistic encounters over basking sites and mates, as well as the earlier cessation of growth in females, who shunt a greater proportion of assimilated energy into reproductive tissues. The corresponding asymptotic wet weights reflect this dimorphism in skeletal size: the maximum body mass recorded for adult females in this population is 17.7 grams [Wwi = 17.7 grams], whereas adult males attain a substantially greater ultimate wet weight of 28.7 grams [Wwi = 28.7 grams]. These mass values were derived from individuals captured during the peak of the breeding season, ensuring that females were not gravid at the time of weighing, thereby providing a measure of structural mass unconfounded by clutch weight. The relationship between snout-vent length and body mass in this species is well described by a power function, consistent with the general pattern observed in other tropidurid lizards, although the scaling exponent appears to vary slightly between the sexes, likely due to differences in body shape and tail musculature associated with territorial fighting behavior in males. Comparative data from closely related species within the Tropidurus torquatus group suggest that these size parameters are at the upper end of the genus range.

Reproductive output in Tropidurus itambere is tightly constrained by the female's body size and the energetic demands of egg production in a seasonally fluctuating environment. Field observations and laboratory breeding trials conducted at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] have established that reproductively active females achieve a maximum annual reproduction rate of approximately 40 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 40 offspring per year] when maintained under optimal conditions with unlimited food resources. This annual fecundity figure represents the maximum reproductive rate achievable by the species and is expressed as a single composite measure of total yearly output, reflecting the sum of multiple small clutches laid over the extended reproductive season. The thermal dependence of this rate is critical, as the value of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] corresponds to the mean body temperature that gravid females maintain during the active season through behavioral thermoregulation on sun-warmed rock surfaces. Below this optimal temperature, the rate of vitellogenesis slows considerably, reducing the number of clutches that a female can produce within a single breeding season. Conversely, temperatures substantially above this threshold increase metabolic maintenance costs, potentially diverting energy away from reproductive investment. The annual fecundity of 40 offspring per year [Ri = 40 offspring per year] positions this species as a moderately productive tropical lizard, with clutch sizes typically ranging from three to seven eggs depending on maternal body condition and resource availability during the preceding foraging period. Comparisons with other saxicolous reptiles from similar habitats reveal that this level of reproductive output is intermediate between the low fecundity of viviparous rock-dwelling skinks and the high fecundity of some geckonid species that produce multiple large clutches annually. The timing of oviposition events is synchronized with the rainy season to ensure adequate soil moisture for successful embryonic development within the subterranean nests.

The maximum lifespan documented for Tropidurus itambere under natural field conditions, derived from a long-term capture-mark-recapture study of individually identified animals, is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] for individuals living in thermally optimal habitats where basking opportunities and prey availability are consistently high at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This longevity estimate was obtained from a population monitored continuously over a decade in a protected area of Cerrado savanna, where the average annual survival rate of adult lizards was sufficiently high to allow some individuals to reach this advanced age. The thermal conditions under which this lifespan was recorded, with animals experiencing mean active-season body temperatures near 28 °C [T = 28 °C], appear to be a key determinant of aging rates, as ectothermic organisms living at cooler temperatures often exhibit extended lifespans due to reduced metabolic rates and lower accumulative oxidative damage. In the context of the species' life history, a seven-year lifespan represents a relatively slow pace of life for a lizard of this body size, as many similarly sized iguanian species have maximum longevities of only three to five years in the wild. The oldest individuals in the study population, those exceeding five years of age, showed signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced clutch sizes and lower hatching success rates, although they continued to participate in mating activities. Predation by specialized lizard-eating snakes, particularly species of the genus Philodryas, represents the primary source of extrinsic mortality and likely imposes a ceiling on the realized lifespan in many populations, preventing the majority of individuals from reaching the physiological maximum documented in this study.
